title_original: David Sims Finally Shows His Archive in Spain
excerpt_original: He has photographed Kate Moss and David Bowie, shot campaigns for the grandest names in luxury, and his work sits in the Tate's collection. On the eve of his sixtieth birthday, the British fashion photographer is at last allowing himself a major exhibition of his archive, at the…

blocks.text: He has photographed Kate Moss and David Bowie, shot campaigns for the grandest names in luxury, and his work sits in the Tate’s collection. On the eve of his sixtieth birthday, the British fashion photographer is at last allowing himself a major exhibition of his archive, at the MOP Foundation in A Coruña, on Spain’s Atlantic coast.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by David Sims.

Born in 1966 in Sheffield, the steel city of northern England, David Sims left school early and assisted the fashion photographers Robert Erdmann and Norman Watson. He went freelance in 1989, worked for the Japanese designer Yohji Yamamoto, and was named young fashion photographer of the year at the Hyères festival as early as 1994.

Britain’s independent style magazines, The Face , i-D , and Dazed & Confused , ran his first editorials. In 1999, for the German house Jil Sander, he photographed the Polish model Malgosia Bela, shoulders bare and hair whipped across her face, her mouth slightly open, in a black and white steeped in end-of-century sensuality.

The timelessness of these portraits is disorienting: the ones from the nineties could run in this year’s magazines without raising an eyebrow. For Vogue Italia , in 2019, he perched the model Jagi Nelson atop a metal ladder. The figure cuts against an enormous sky, and the grainy texture lends the scene the air of a memory. His pictures, says Marta Ortega Pérez, the founder of MOP, have brought together “cultural movements that have defined successive generations.”

blocks.caption: Roisin, Souvenir St Moritz, 2022 © David Sim

blocks.text: Near St. Moritz, in 2022, he staged the model Róisín Salmon. Propped against a boulder, dressed head to toe in black, a can raised to her lips and her eyes closed, she seems to have left the world behind. Advertising rarely permits that much abandon. The founder praises in David Sims a steady devotion to youth culture, to “its energy, vulnerability, creativity and capacity for change.”

After thirty-five years of work, David Sims had never really opened the archive. The show abandons chronology and begins in the late nineties, just before film gave way to digital. It offers, the founder promises, a chance to see the work “from David’s own perspective.” These pictures, built to last the life of a single issue, will hold the walls for five months.

blocks.caption: Poster for "The Hamster Becomes The Problem" © David Sims

blocks.text: “The Hamster Becomes The Problem,” by David Sims, is on view at the MOP Center in A Coruña, Spain, from November 21, 2026, to May 1, 2027. Admission is free.
